facts.statement: Pelagornis fossils date from the Late Oligocene to the Early Pleistocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Oligocene–Early Pleistocene (Chattian–Gelasian)

facts.statement: The genus Pelagornis was described by Lartet in 1857.
facts.quote: authority: Lartet, 1857

facts.statement: Pelagornis is an extinct genus of pseudotooth birds.
facts.quote: Pelagornis is an extinct genus of prehistoric pseudotooth birds, a group of extinct seabirds.

facts.statement: Pelagornis sandersi holds the record for the widest wingspan of any bird known.
facts.quote: Members of Pelagornis represent among the largest pseudotooth birds, with one species, P. sandersi, having the widest wingspan of any bird known.

facts.statement: The type species Pelagornis miocaenus is known from 23 million-year-old sediments.
facts.quote: The type species Pelagornis miocaenus is known from 23 MA Aquitanian (Early Miocene) sediments

facts.statement: The species Pelagornis mauretanicus was named in 2008.
facts.quote: Pelagornis mauretanicus was only named in 2008.

facts.statement: Remains of Pelagornis mauretanicus were found in 2.5 million-year-old deposits in Morocco.
facts.quote: Its remains have been found in 2.5 Ma Gelasian (Late Pliocene/Early Pleistocene, MN17) deposits at Ahl al Oughlam (Morocco).

facts.statement: Pelagornis sandersi was described in July 2014 from remains dating to 25 million years ago.
facts.quote: Pelagornis sandersi, whose fossil remains date from 25 million years ago during the Chattian age of the Oligocene, was described in July 2014.

facts.statement: The only known fossil of Pelagornis sandersi was uncovered in 1983 by James Malcom at Charleston International Airport.
facts.quote: The only known fossil of P. sandersi was first uncovered in 1983 at Charleston International Airport, South Carolina, discovered by James Malcom, while working construction building a new terminal there.

facts.statement: The fossil of Pelagornis sandersi was rediscovered by Daniel T. Ksepka in 2010 after being stored at the Charleston Museum.
facts.quote: After excavation, the fossil of P. sandersi was catalogued and put in storage at the Charleston Museum, where it remained until it was rediscovered by paleontologist Daniel T. Ksepka in 2010.

facts.statement: Pelagornis sandersi is named after Albert Sanders, who led the excavation of the fossil.
facts.quote: The bird is named after Albert Sanders, the former curator of natural history at the Charleston Museum, who led the excavation of P. sandersi.

facts.statement: Pelagornis was initially thought to be related to albatrosses but is now classified in the Pelecaniformes.
facts.quote: Like many pseudotooth birds, it was initially believed to be related to the albatrosses in the tube-nosed seabirds (Procellariiformes), but subsequently placed in the Pelecaniformes

facts.statement: The family name Pelagornithidae has largely replaced Pseudodontornithidae for pseudotooth birds.
facts.quote: In any case, the family name of the pseudotooth birds, Pelagornithidae, as the senior synonym has widely replaced the once-commonly used Pseudodontornithidae.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Pacific fossils may represent a species distinct from P. miocaenus or closer to Osteodontornis.
facts.quote: Given the distance in space and time involved, all Pacific material may well have been a species different from P. miocaenus or even from birds closer to Osteodontornis.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Pseudodontornis belongs to a distinct lineage, which might require revalidating the family name Pseudodontornithidae.
facts.quote: It may be that Pseudodontornis belongs to a distinct lineage of these birds, and then the family name would perhaps be revalidated.

facts.statement: The largest known species, P. sandersi, had an estimated wingspan between 6.06 and 7.38 meters.
facts.quote: The sole specimen of P. sandersi has a wingspan estimated between approximately 6.06 and 7.38 m

facts.statement: P. sandersi holds the record for the largest wingspan of any flying bird ever discovered, approximately twice that of the modern wandering albatross.
facts.quote: giving it the largest wingspan of any flying bird yet discovered, twice that of the wandering albatross

facts.statement: The species P. chilensis weighed between 16 and 29 kilograms and had a wingspan exceeding 5.2 meters.
facts.quote: Although smaller than P. sandersi, P. chilensis was estimated at 16 to 29 kg weight and over 5.2 m wingspan

facts.statement: P. miocaenus likely had a head length of about 40 cm and a wingspan ranging from over 5 meters to perhaps 6 meters.
facts.quote: Its head would have been about 40 cm long in life, and its wingspan was probably more than 5 m, perhaps closer to 6 m

facts.statement: P. sandersi possessed tooth-like or knob-like extensions on its bill known as "pseudo-teeth" to help grip slippery prey.
facts.quote: P. sandersi had tooth-like or knob-like extensions of the bill's margin, called "pseudo-teeth"

facts.statement: Researcher Ksepka noted that the pseudo-teeth of P. sandersi lacked enamel, did not grow in sockets, and were not lost or replaced during the bird's life.
facts.quote: According to Ksepka, the teeth of P. sandersi "don't have enamel, they don't grow in sockets, and they aren't lost and replaced throughout the creature's life span."

facts.statement: Unlike Osteodontornis, Pelagornis featured a single smaller pseudo-tooth between each pair of large pseudo-teeth, similar to the older Pseudodontornis.
facts.quote: Unlike in its contemporary Osteodontornis but like in the older Pseudodontornis, Pelagornis had a single smaller "tooth" between each two large "teeth".

facts.statement: Pelagornis possessed extremely large and well-developed salt glands located inside its eye sockets.
facts.quote: The salt glands inside the eye sockets were extremely large and well-developed in Pelagornis.

facts.statement: P. sandersi had short, stumpy legs and likely flew by hopping off cliff edges rather than taking off from flat ground.
facts.quote: P. sandersi had short, stumpy legs, and was probably only able to fly by hopping off cliff edges.

facts.statement: It is estimated that P. sandersi could fly at speeds of up to 60 km/h.
facts.quote: It has been estimated that it was able to fly at up to 60 km/h.

facts.statement: Due to its large size, P. sandersi likely moulted all of its flight feathers simultaneously, a behavior similar to ducks, geese, or grebes.
facts.quote: Due to the size of P. sandersi, the bird likely moulted all of its flight feathers at once, similarly to Anseriformes (ducks and geese) or grebes

facts.statement: Pelagornis was not a skim-feeder because it could not generate enough energy to overcome the drag required for skimming prey from the ocean surface.
facts.quote: Pelagornis was not a skim-feeder like members of the genus Rynchops (skimmers), as it could not meet the energy requirements for skim-feeding.

facts.statement: Dan Ksepka identified fossils belonging to a new species and suggested that P. sandersi could fly due to its relatively small body mass combined with its long wings.
facts.quote: Dan Ksepka of the National Evolutionary Synthesis Center in Durham, North Carolina, who identified that the discovered fossils belonged to a new species, thinks it was able to fly in part because of its relatively small body and long wings

facts.statement: The genus Pelagornis was originally described in 1857 by the French paleontologist and geologist Édouard Lartet.
facts.quote: Este género fue descrito originalmente en el año 1857 por el paleontólogo y geólogo francés Édouard Lartet.

facts.statement: The genus is divided into four species: P. chilensis (Mayr & Rubilar, 2010), P. mauretanicus (Mourer-Chauviré & Geraads, 2008), P. miocaenus (Lartet, 1857), and P. sandersi (Ksepka, 2014).
facts.quote: Se subdivide en 4 especies: Pelagornis chilensis Mayr & Rubilar, 2010 Pelagornis mauretanicus Mourer-Chauviré & Geraads, 2008 Pelagornis miocaenus Lartet, 1857 Pelagornis sandersi Ksepka, 2014

facts.statement: Species of Pelagornis lived from the Late Oligocene to the Early Pleistocene, spanning from 25 to 2.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Mantuvo especies vivientes desde el Oligoceno superior y el Pleistoceno temprano, es decir, desde los 25 hasta los 2,5 millones de años atrás.

facts.statement: The genus Pelagornis existed from the Bartonian to the Piacenzian, between 41.03 and 2.58 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Bartonian to Piacenzian (41.03 to 2.58 million years ago)

facts.statement: Fossils of Pelagornis have been found in the Eocene Aridal Formation in Morocco and the La Meseta Formation on Seymour Island, Antarctica.
facts.quote: Fossils of Pelagornis have been found in: Eocene Aridal Formation (Bartonian), Morocco La Meseta Formation, Seymour Island, Antarctica

facts.statement: Fossils of Pelagornis have been found in the Oligocene Chandler Bridge Formation in South Carolina, USA.
facts.quote: Oligocene Chandler Bridge Formation, South Carolina, USA

facts.statement: Fossils of Pelagornis have been found in Miocene deposits across Australia, Chile, France, the USA, New Zealand, Peru, Portugal, and Venezuela.
facts.quote: Miocene Black Rock Sandstone, Australia Bahía Inglesa Formation (Mayoan-Montehermosan), Chile Molasse Coquilliere Formation, France Calvert Formation, Virginia, USA Waipara River mouth (Waiauan), Canterbury, New Zealand Pisco Formation (Chasicoan-Huayquerian), Peru Costa da Caparica or Fonte de Pipa, Tagus Basin, Portugal Castillo (Colhuehuapian-Santacrucian) and Capadare Formations (Laventan-Mayoan), Venezuela

facts.statement: Fossils of Pelagornis have been found in Pliocene formations in New Zealand, California, and North Carolina, USA.
facts.quote: Pliocene Greta Formation, New Zealand Purisima Formation, California and Yorktown Formation, North Carolina, USA

facts.statement: Fossils of Pelagornis have been found in the Early Pleistocene Ahl al Oughlam formation in Morocco.
facts.quote: Early Pleistocene Ahl al Oughlam, Morocco

facts.statement: There was originally a scientific debate regarding whether P. sandersi was capable of flight.
facts.quote: Originally, there were controversies over whether or not P. sandersi would be able to fly.

facts.statement: Some scientists were surprised that P. sandersi could fly, as its weight of 21.9 to 40.1 kg exceeded the limits predicted by predominant theories of bird flight mechanics.
facts.quote: Some scientists expressed surprise at the idea that this species could fly at all, given that, at between 21.9 and 40.1 kg, it would be considered too heavy by the predominant theory of the mechanism by which birds fly.

facts.statement: Research published in 2026 by Hellyer-Price, Venditti, and Humphries argues that Pelagornis was likely unable to skim-feed based on drag calculations.
facts.quote: Hellyer-Price, Venditti & Humphries (2026) calculate the drag on the bill of Pelagornis while skimming, and argue that the studied bird was likely unable to skim-feed.

facts.statement: Goedert et al. (2026) reported the discovery of a Pelagornis orri braincase from the Miocene Astoria Formation in Oregon and isolated bones from the Eocene Keasey Formation, representing one of the oldest pelagornithid records.
facts.quote: Goedert et al. (2026) report the discovery of a braincase of Pelagornis orri from the Miocene Astoria Formation (Oregon, United States), providing new information on the anatomy of the species, as well as discovery of isolated vertebra and phalanx bone of Pelagornis sp. from the Eocene Keasey Formation (Oregon), representing one of the oldest pelagornithid records reported to date.

rejected.statement: The original specimen of Pelagornis miocaenus was a left humerus almost the size of a human arm.
rejected.quote: The original specimen on which P. miocaenus was founded was a left humerus almost the size of a human arm.

rejected.statement: It is debated whether South American fossils of similar size and age belong to one or two species.
rejected.quote: It is not clear whether the South American fossils, of similar size and age and not including directly comparable bones, are from one or two species.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'South American fossils of similar size and age'

rejected.statement: P. miocaenus was one of the largest pseudotooth birds, comparable in size to Osteodontornis and the older Dasornis.
rejected.quote: P. miocaenus was one of the largest pseudotooth birds, hardly smaller in size than Osteodontornis or the older Dasornis
